structure.title: A return from war
structure.text: Agamemnon brings the public victory at Troy into a household with unresolved claims against its returning king.

structure.title: Inherited obligations and judgment
structure.text: The Libation Bearers and The Eumenides follow the demands passed to another generation and the search for a way to judge them.

people.name: Clytemnestra
people.text: The queen of Argos, who has ruled for ten years while her husband fought at Troy, and who has not forgotten what he did before he sailed.

people.name: Orestes
people.text: Agamemnon's son, sent away as a child, who returns grown to a house where he is told his duty and his crime may be the same act.

people.name: The Furies
people.text: Ancient goddesses who hunt down anyone who sheds kindred blood, and who refuse to give up their claim when younger gods try to overrule them.

context.title: A family before the opening
context.text: The war's departure required Agamemnon's sacrifice of his daughter Iphigenia. That earlier act remains part of the homecoming.
context.takeaway: Victory does not erase an unpaid grievance.

context.title: Three linked plays
context.text: Each play changes the setting in which justice is demanded. Read the trilogy as a developing problem, not three independent verdicts.
context.takeaway: Notice what a new forum makes possible.

notice.why: Opposing actions can claim the same moral authority.
Communal anxiety fills gaps that no observer can settle immediately.

opening: The war is over, and Agamemnon is coming home to a wife who remembers what he sacrificed to get his ships to Troy. Victory has not settled the debt inside the family. Aeschylus follows a succession of people who can justify their next act of violence by pointing to the last one. Across three plays, the need to punish becomes a problem that revenge cannot finish solving, and the possibility of judgment by a community has to contend with grievances that will not quietly disappear.
